  collapse = TRUE,

```{r setup}
library(mysteryroster)
```

`attribute_agreement()` (`vignette("attribute-agreement")`) and
`attribute_lead_lag_matrix()` (`vignette("lead-lag-staleness")`) both
compare exactly two sources at a time. With three or more, two further
relative claims become available -- still never "this source is
correct," only claims about the *group*: how much of it agrees, whether
that agreement holds up over time, and which source the group tends to
converge toward.

The first two functions below were ported from a one-off script
(`build_cross_source_comparison.R`) written for a midwifery workforce
audit outside this package, then generalized past that script's
hardcoded assumption of exactly four sources and a fixed 2021--2025
window.

## How much of the group agrees?

Four simulated sources for three NPIs. NPI 1 is unanimous; NPI 2 splits
two ways with no agreeing pair; NPI 3 has a 3-of-4 majority:

```{r consensus-tier}
s <- list(
  nppes = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2", "3"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "CO", "TX")),
  dac   = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2", "3"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "NM", "TX")),
  op    = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2", "3"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "NM", "OK")),
  pecos = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2", "3"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "CO", "TX"))
)
attribute_consensus_tier(s, attribute = "state")
```

NPI 2's two pairs that happen to agree (`dac`/`op` on `NM`) still only
reach 2 of 4 sources -- not a strict majority, so it is `"split"`, not
`"majority"`. No value is ever picked as the group's answer; only the
size of the largest agreeing group is reported.

## Does that consensus hold up over time?

Given a tier classification for each identifier in each year (for
example, `attribute_consensus_tier()`'s own output, run once per year
and stacked), `attribute_consensus_tier_flow()` counts year-over-year
transitions between tiers -- a claim about *stability*, not about who
moved:

```{r consensus-flow}
tiers <- data.frame(
  id   = rep(c("1", "2", "3"), 2),
  year = rep(c(2023, 2024), each = 3),
  tier = c("unanimous", "split", "majority", "unanimous", "unanimous", "split")
)
attribute_consensus_tier_flow(tiers)
```

NPI 1 stayed unanimous both years; NPI 2 resolved from split to
unanimous; NPI 3 degraded from majority to split. By default
(`require_all_years = TRUE`) the flow is restricted to identifiers
present in every year supplied, so apparent churn is never actually
just sources entering or leaving the comparison.

## Which source does the group converge toward?

`attribute_lead_lag_matrix()` answers "who moved first" for one pair.
Aggregating across every pair of three or more sources gives a
per-source ranking: how often did *other* sources eventually adopt this
one's value, versus how often did this source get corrected toward
someone else's? Source `b` below already has the value that `a` and `c`
both move toward:

```{r corroboration}
a <- data.frame(npi = c("1", "1"), year = c(2022, 2023), state = c("CO", "NM"))
b <- data.frame(npi = c("1", "1"), year = c(2022, 2023), state = c("NM", "NM"))
c <- data.frame(npi = c("1", "1"), year = c(2022, 2023), state = c("CO", "NM"))
attribute_source_corroboration(list(a = a, b = b, c = c), attributes = "state")
```

`b`'s `lead_rate` of 1 says the rest of this small comparison set
converged toward it -- not that `b` is correct, only that it is the one
others caught up to, across the `n_pairs` opportunities it actually had.
A pair that shares no overlapping years is skipped with a message
rather than failing the whole call:

```{r corroboration-skip}
d <- data.frame(npi = "1", year = 2025, state = "CO") # no year in common with a or b
suppressWarnings(attribute_source_corroboration(list(a = a, b = b, d = d), attributes = "state"))
```

## Is exactly one source the odd one out?

`attribute_consensus_tier()` reports a 4-source 2-2 split and a
genuine 3-1 lone dissenter the same way: both are `"split"`, since
neither has a strict majority. `attribute_odd_one_out()` draws that
distinction explicitly -- a lone dissenter is a narrower, structurally
different claim than "no majority exists":

```{r odd-one-out}
s <- list(
  nppes = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "CO")),
  dac   = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "CO")),
  op    = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2"), year = 2024, state = c("NM", "NM")),
  pecos = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "NM"))
)
records <- attribute_odd_one_out(s, attribute = "state")
records[, c("id", "n_distinct_values", "structure", "odd_source")]
```

NPI 1 (`CO, CO, NM, CO`) has a lone dissenter (`op`); NPI 2
(`CO, CO, NM, NM`) is a tied 2-2 split, deliberately *not* reported as
`odd_one_out` even though it also has two distinct values.
`attribute_odd_one_out_rate()` tallies this across identifiers into a
per-source rate, giving every source a row -- including a `0` rate --
rather than omitting sources that happened never to be the outlier:

```{r odd-one-out-rate}
attribute_odd_one_out_rate(records)
```

`op` and `pecos` are each the lone dissenter in exactly one of their
two eligible identifier-years; `nppes` and `dac` never are. None of
this says `op` or `pecos` is wrong -- only that each sat outside a
value the other three shared, once.

## Does agreement differ by some other covariate?

`attribute_agreement_by_spell_age()` stratifies by one specific thing:
how long a value has sat unchanged. `attribute_agreement_by_covariate()`
generalizes the same question to any grouping variable -- rurality,
provider type, years since licensure, or anything else with one value
per identifier, pulled from a third data frame rather than assumed to
live in either source being compared:

```{r covariate}
source_a <- data.frame(npi = c("1", "2", "3"), state = c("CO", "NY", "TX"))
source_b <- data.frame(npi = c("1", "2", "3"), state = c("CO", "NJ", "TX"))
rurality <- data.frame(npi = c("1", "2", "3"), setting = c("rural", "urban", "urban"))
attribute_agreement_by_covariate(source_a, source_b, rurality,
                                  attribute = "state", covariate = "setting")
```

Passing a continuous covariate works the same way once it is binned
(for example with `cut()`); the function itself never auto-bins, so
whatever strata the input carries are exactly what gets reported.

## How much does a small sample narrow the claim?

Every percentage in this vignette -- `concordance_pct`, `pct_agree`,
`agree_pct` -- is a point estimate. `wilson_ci()` turns an agreement
count into a confidence interval, handling small `n` and extreme rates
better than a normal approximation:

```{r wilson}
wilson_ci(n_agree = 9, n_compared = 10)
```

Ten comparable identifier-years at 90% agreement could plausibly be
anywhere from 60% to 98% -- a much wider claim than "90%" alone
suggests. `attribute_agreement_add_ci()` attaches this directly to an
existing table rather than extracting and recombining columns by hand;
`as_percent` matches whichever scale that table already uses
(`attribute_agreement_summary()`'s `pct_agree` is a proportion,
`attribute_consensus_tier()`'s `concordance_pct` a percentage):

```{r wilson-attach}
s2 <- list(
  a = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "CO")),
  b = data.frame(npi = c("1", "2"), year = 2024, state = c("CO", "NM"))
)
attribute_agreement_add_ci(attribute_agreement_summary(attribute_agreement(s2, attribute = "state")))
```

With only 2 comparable identifier-years, the interval spans nearly the
whole `[0, 1]` range -- an honest reflection of how little a 50%
agreement rate on `n = 2` actually supports.

## What this layer does and doesn't add

A high concordance tier, a stable flow, a high corroboration rate, or a
narrow confidence interval are all still relative claims about the
comparison set, not about truth -- a value every source agrees on can
still be wrong if every source traces back to the same original error
(see `vignette("attribute-agreement")`'s note on two sources agreeing
on a stale value). What this layer adds over the pairwise functions is
scale -- a claim about the whole group at once -- and, with
`wilson_ci()`, an honest sense of how much any of these percentages
should actually be trusted given how many identifier-years back them.
